commenti.body: [removed]

Well it's like this: If you want a somewhat coherent story, you can either show the brilliant strategist, or the dictator who fired cannons at women and children at point-blank range. The movie chooses to show a Napoleon who is kind of Trump-like, extremely narcissistic and emotionally immature, with a huge oedipus complex. That analogy probably holds up partly, and it's refreshing to see a biopic that's openly critical of its subject. 

\[Oh, And the movie is one of those, that suffers from the fact, that is effectively an 8-hour miniseries cut down to feature length \[stares angrily in Scorsese's direction\].

I just found it aimless narrative-wise at multiple points… the film doesn’t provide a development for him or his relationship with Josephine, and the audience is just thrown in a bunch of scenes without a clear point of focus. Scarpa might be more to blame on this than Scott? Anyways… beyond the mastery the latter would have on an epic as this would have been, I also see a lost opportunity

OPs point is that of those options you discuss, Scott went with the one that fails to highlight a rather incredible life in incredible times. A missed opportunity to say the least.  And your point to poke fun at his Trump-like behaviors seems awfully reductive. Sure Napoleon had faults and failures, nobody would disagree, but you still can cover those without downplaying the clearly supreme aspects of his Generalship and ambitions.

Disappointed it isn’t an epic film on the life and times of an endlessly interesting, successful, and destructive person.

Showing multiple sides to someone is fairly boilerplate for a biopic. As a genre, it may land on the positive/propaganda side, but we got another biopic this year about a man who changed the world that, in a similar runtime, reckoned with a breadth of his qualities, including sexual proclivities that might embarrass.

I don’t think you’re wrong to make the Trump analogy. I can see Phoenix thinking precisely that. Whats remarkable, again, is reducing a man who’s probably paralleled by five or six others in recorded history as “Trump-like”. Whether that narcissistic reduction flows from America or British Isles, it’s beneath it’s subject. If they were interested in why the public might chuck out a minted elite for some upstart, that might’ve been interesting. But that’s not a Scott movie. Which is perfectly alright. I just think there is a Scott movie on Napoleon that wasn’t made. Or is hiding again in a Directors Cut.

If this film was some kind of answer to Napoleon propaganda it would make more sense. In context it’s supposed to have an air of definitiveness. A great director. One of the great actors of the era. In a time where the public has shown increased interest in this man of history for reasons that are far more interesting and worthy of exploration than whatever Scott or Phoenix are up to
applying today's moral standarts to the people pre 1900s is dumb as hell.

Precisely. Its central assertion is about the importance of Josephine to Napoleon and it manages to provide us ample scenes for that claim to be justified but never once supplies a real emotion within them. Emotion is not Scotts forte but he’s done it before. The scenes just sit there. Their relationship features assertions of why she is important to him and we sense he believes this, but we never are made to understand why. Given that this assertion is something of a slight as well, packaged within Napoleon’s being made a literal cuck before the French public, it seems more apart of the comedy than anything deep
[removed]

Napoleon as Trump seems incredibly unfair.  Napoleon cemented a large part of the Enlightenment vision.  Equality before the law, merit-based promotion, sweeping away the Ancien Régime.   There won't be a Trump equivalent of the Napoleonic Code.   Napoleon as tyrant is an image cultivated by those he fought against, which were not exactly liberal democratic regimes.

I left the theater afterwards telling my friend that it didn't feel like we really got to see what made napoleon great.  There he is at all the famous stops, but how did he get there? He feels like just any other General officer of the time.  I was really hoping to see how they portrayed Napoleon as a motivator and an influencer who managed to get the entire french army to follow him with vigorous enthusiasm.  It felt like he was just in the right place at the right time, and what he did could have been achieved by plenty of other people in his circumstances

Recently a lot of poorly received films have been said to be  “actually comedies”..   I just don’t buy it. If they were, it would be obvious. 

Hollywood doesn’t put millions into a project for 10% of the audience to “get it” and the rest to just think it was boring or lacked more interesting plot points.  

Looking at you “the killer”

It’s a reflection of the modern world. Look at any form of media and women’s empowerment is a running theme. You can’t have a story about an intelligent and cunning man because it just doesn’t fit the narrative.
I also told my partner “did it come through that Napoleon basically ruled continental Europe for 10 or so years?”. From the untrained viewer’s POV he won a few battles and became emperor.
[removed]
The disrespect to Scorsese, wow.
The jump from Consol to Emperor is laughable, especially considered he scoffed at the suggestion of him being king. This movie is such a non entertaining mess

Of all tales this has to be among the most brain-dead. I really don't think Scarpa's lackluster screenplay and Scott inability to portray this relationship is because they couldn't do otherwise. Sure, women empowerment is one of the many arguments of the zeitgeist, but to suggest that you can't deviate from it is tin foiled hat crap for the Facebook boomer folk.

Yeah, I'm going back and rewatching some documentaries about napoleon I watched in preparation for the film.  He apparently gave enormous weight to logistical type circumstances that others of the time hadn't even considered.  I was really hoping for some scenes where he eloquently shows off his perception for all things that influence war by shooting down a bunch of other people's seemingly smart ideas and then demonstrate how he knows best.  I can't stress it enough. In the movie, he pretty much does what would mostly be expected of an officer of the time.  Perhaps a bit better than most.  We didn't even get to see a map of France from before and after Napoleon took the helm.  I didn't hate the movie.  Not at all. What's good, was great.  But I wanted the whole thing to be great.
Go ahead. Nothing will convince me, Gangs of New York is not a 8-hour miniseries that has been butchered to make a movie.
It's not? Miniseries weren't even such a thing in those years. Just a movie fucked by its producer. Whatever, I don't want to interrupt your crazy flow.

Okay but we still end up with half a movie about Josephine and very little about the military and political genius of Bonaparte. Frankly he’s portrayed as a petulant child. I’m not suggesting you can’t deviate from the current zeitgeist, but you have to admit most media is saturated in this idea.

There would be nothing wrong with having a movie about Josephine, the concept at the bone is interesting and less already seen than the standard biopic. The problem lies elsewhere which is that it's half a movie about the marriage and half about the Wikipedia page. And yes, he's portrayed as a petulant child, and had the movie fully explored the idea or backed it through substance, instead of forgetting it every two scenes, that wouldn't have been the problem.

"Most media is saturated" yes, just like you can find some kind of "propaganda" and cultural marks in every single decade of film. In most cases it's just a marketing tool to make people talk about the film, in this case it's just a shitty script that couldn't choose what it wanted to be.

I also recently saw The Killer. Both Napoleon and The Killer rely a great deal on irony. They’re not “comedies” in the classically American sense. I saw The Killer with an audience. People were laughing the whole time. Not “why is this so bad” laughter but aware that things were being played for laughs. Both movies share a mocking perspective on their titular characters. You’re never rooting for either of them.

For what it’s worth I liked neither film
